items.answer: Not supported. The paper says tier is an imperfect proxy for safety risk. Tier assignments are approximate, languages within a tier can be represented very differently in a given model's training data, and transliteration vulnerability depends on script rather than tier.
rubric: Answers not supported (or contradicted).
Cites that tier is an approximate and imperfect proxy, with within-tier variation across models and/or script-conditioned effects.

items.question: Equation 1 divides by the number of harmful prompts in the cell. Suppose that denominator is taken literally while incoherent responses are dropped from the count of successes. In which direction would heavy coherence filtering move a cell's ASR, and why?
items.answer: It would push ASR downward. An incoherent response can never count as a success but would still sit in the denominator, so it behaves exactly like a refusal. Exclusion is neutral only if the denominator is restricted to coherent responses.
rubric: Asserts that ASR would be biased downward (deflated) by heavy filtering under the literal reading.
Explains that filtered responses stay in the denominator without being able to count as successes, so they act like refusals.
Notes that the bias disappears only if the denominator counts coherent responses alone.

items.question: Code-switched prompts are mostly English with a short translated span. Suppose a model mirrors this style and answers in a mix of English and the target language. How could the coherence filter mishandle such answers?
items.answer: Mixed-language text can split language identification, giving confidence below 0.3 or detecting a third language. A coherent reply could then be marked incoherent and dropped. This would shrink and bias the code-switching cells for reasons unrelated to output quality.
rubric: Asserts that coherent mixed-language replies may be wrongly flagged as incoherent and excluded.
Explains this via langdetect confidence below 0.3 or a misdetected language caused by mixing two languages.
States that code-switching cells would then rest on fewer or skewed responses (a selection bias).

items.question: Suppose a language's harmfulness probe direction were exactly the negative of the English one. What first principal angle would Figure 4 report, and why would that be misleading for an English-calibrated intervention?
items.answer: It would report 0°, because subspaces and principal angles ignore the sign of a direction. Yet the two languages' harmful sides would lie in opposite senses along that axis. An intervention applied along the English direction with the English sign would act backwards for that language.
rubric: Asserts that the angle would be 0° (subspaces look perfectly aligned).
Explains that principal angles between subspaces are sign-invariant, so a flipped orientation is invisible.
Notes that an English-calibrated intervention would push in the wrong sense for that language.

items.question: Row 2 of Figure 9 compares a harm signal at t_inst with a refusal signal at t_post. Why could a mismatch between these two signals fail to show that harm and refusal are represented separately?
items.answer: The two signals are read at different token positions. A difference between them could reflect how representations change across positions rather than two distinct encodings. The analysis is also correlational, with no patching to separate the two.
rubric: Asserts that the mismatch does not by itself establish separate representations.
Explains that the signals come from different token positions, so position is a confound.
Optionally notes that the panels are correlational, with no activation patching.

items.question: The cross-lingual term in Eq. 3 averages a direction's harmful-harmless margin over the non-English languages. When would a direction with a respectable average cross-lingual margin still be a poor reference for some of those languages?
items.answer: This happens when the margin is large in some languages but near zero or even negative (reversed) in others. Positive and negative margins partly cancel in the average, so the loss term cannot reveal the problem. Only per-language margins, as in Figure 6, would show it.
rubric: Asserts that the average can hide languages with near-zero or reversed (negative) margins.
Explains that the term is a mean, so large margins elsewhere offset or cancel weak or negative ones.
Points to per-language margins (Figure 6) as the needed check.

items.question: Figure 4 plots principal angles per tier. Given the benchmark's script composition, when would the Tier-3 curve misrepresent its member languages?
items.answer: Tier 3 contains one Devanagari language (Hindi) and three Latin-script languages (Turkish, Indonesian, Swahili). If script affects alignment with English, Hindi's angles would differ from the others. The averaged curve would then blend a script effect with resource level and describe none of the languages well.
rubric: Asserts that the Tier-3 average can misrepresent individual languages when Hindi behaves differently from the rest.
Explains that Hindi is the only non-Latin-script language in Tier 3, so the average mixes script with resource level.

items.question: Why might the gap between translationese and standard-translation ASR grow with tier even if models were equally sensitive to machine-translation surface statistics in every language?
items.answer: Translationese adds two more machine-translation steps, and how much a round trip drifts depends on translation quality. Quality is lower for low-resource languages. Low-tier translationese prompts would therefore differ more from their standard versions, through larger semantic drift or errors, and not only in surface statistics. The French example drifts only slightly.
rubric: Asserts that the gap could grow with tier for reasons other than sensitivity to surface statistics.
Explains that round-trip drift scales with translation quality, which is worse for lower tiers, so low-tier translationese prompts change more.

items.question: Why does it matter that resource tiers were defined from training-data availability rather than from the benchmark's own results?
items.answer: Tiers defined by observed ASR would make any tier gradient circular. Because tiers are fixed externally, a gradient along them is a genuine empirical pattern. The grouping is also the same for every model, so per-tier aggregates can be compared across models.
rubric: Asserts that external definition avoids circularity: a gradient is a finding rather than an artifact of how tiers were drawn.
Explains that ASR-defined tiers would guarantee a gradient, while a fixed external grouping also gives a common axis across models.

items.question: In the Japanese code-switching example in Appendix E, what suggests the differing span was translated piece by piece rather than as a Japanese phrase, and why does this matter for the condition's realism?
items.answer: The translated items are separated by spaces and appear in standalone forms. Examples are 扇動する, または and そして for 'and', with no particles joining them into a grammatical phrase, which fits translating each alphabetic token on its own. The result is word salad inside an English frame, not natural code-switching, which illustrates the caveat that automated perturbations may not reflect human code-switching.
rubric: Identifies evidence of token-by-token translation, such as space-separated words, dictionary or standalone forms, or no joining particles.
Concludes that the code-switched prompts are unnatural, linking this to the caveat that they may not reflect real human code-switching.

items.question: Why are within-model comparisons across languages less affected by the problems that make cross-model ASR magnitudes incomparable, and which problem still remains?
items.answer: Refusal style belongs to the model and stays roughly constant across its languages. Its interaction with WildGuard therefore largely cancels in within-model comparisons. Back-translation quality, however, varies by language, so even within-model comparisons stay exposed to it, especially for Tier 4.
rubric: Explains that the model's refusal style (and its interaction with WildGuard) is held fixed within a model, so it largely cancels.
States that language-dependent back-translation quality, worst for Tier 4, still affects within-model comparisons.

items.question: For a given model, why should each Tier-4 language's transliteration ASR equal its standard-translation ASR?
items.answer: All Tier-4 languages are non-Romance and written in Latin script, so romanizing them leaves the translated prompt unchanged. With greedy decoding, identical prompts give identical responses, so the scores are the same. This assumes the translation step returns the same text both times and romanization is a true no-op.
rubric: Asserts that the two ASRs should be identical.
Explains that romanizing an already Latin-script, non-Romance language is a no-op, and greedy decoding makes identical inputs give identical outputs.
Notes the condition: same translation output and no changes made by the romanizer (e.g., to diacritics).

items.question: Why can the sharp safety-regime change between Tiers 2 and 3 under standard translation not be explained by how much of each prompt is non-English?
items.answer: Standard translation translates the whole prompt in every language, so prompts are entirely non-English in both tiers. Since that amount does not change across the boundary, the shift must come from factors specific to each language, such as resource level or translation quality.
rubric: Asserts that the amount of non-English text cannot explain the shift.
Explains that standard translation is fully non-English in all tiers, so this amount is constant across the Tier 2/3 boundary.

items.question: A researcher wants to estimate the effect of script while holding resource tier fixed, using only Minionese's languages. Which tiers allow such a comparison and which do not?
items.answer: Tier 1 allows it (Chinese against the Latin-script languages), and so does Tier 3 (Hindi against Turkish, Indonesian and Swahili). Tier 2 is entirely non-Latin and Tier 4 entirely Latin, so they offer no within-tier script contrast. Each usable contrast also rests on a single non-Latin language.
rubric: Identifies Tiers 1 and 3 as allowing within-tier script comparisons (Chinese and Hindi against Latin-script languages).
States that Tiers 2 (all non-Latin) and 4 (all Latin) do not.
Optionally notes that each contrast depends on only one non-Latin language.

items.question: An audit summarizes each language by averaging its ASR over the four Minionese perturbations. Why are German's and Hindi's averages not built from comparable conditions?
items.answer: German is a non-Romance language in Latin script, so its transliteration prompts are the same as its standard translations, and standard translation effectively counts twice. Hindi's transliteration really changes the script. The two averages therefore combine different sets of conditions, which is one reason to report each perturbation separately.
rubric: Explains that German transliteration is a no-op, duplicating standard translation, while Hindi transliteration changes script.
Concludes that the averages weight conditions differently and are not comparable, favoring disaggregated reporting.

items.question: For some language and layer, probe AUC is near 1 but the silhouette score in the harmfulness subspace is near 0. How should a team interpret this?
items.answer: Harmfulness information is present and linearly decodable, because a separating hyperplane exists. However, the two classes form diffuse, overlapping clouds rather than compact clusters. The two measures do not contradict each other: they describe decodability and cluster shape respectively.
rubric: States that harmfulness is linearly decodable (information present, a separating hyperplane exists).
States that the classes are diffuse or non-compact per silhouette, and that this is consistent with high AUC rather than contradictory.

items.question: A team has new harmful prompts in several languages but no harmless counterparts. Which Minionese tools can they still run, and which can they not?
items.answer: The ASR pipeline still works, because ASR uses only harmful prompts. The refusal direction r-hat can still be computed if the model refuses some English prompts and complies with others. Probes, harmfulness subspaces, silhouette, principal angles and cone margins all need a harmful-harmless contrast, so they cannot be run. The code-switching perturbation also needs the differing span between pair members, so it cannot be built either.
rubric: States that ASR and the refusal-based r-hat remain possible, given both refused and complied English responses.
States that probes, subspaces, silhouette, principal angles and cone margins are unavailable because they need harmful-harmless pairs.
Notes that code-switching cannot be constructed without a counterpart defining the differing span.

items.question: A team wants to know whether violence-related and fraud-related harm occupy different directions in a language. Can the paper's harmfulness subspaces answer this as constructed?
items.answer: No. Each subspace is built from probes for only two categories, 'all' and 'unknown', so it has at most two dimensions and none is tied to a specific harm type. The team would need to train a probe for each harm category.
rubric: Asserts that the subspaces as constructed cannot answer it.
Explains that they come from only the 'all' and 'unknown' probes (at most two dimensions, not category-specific), so per-category probes are needed.

items.question: A team wants a cone direction that works specifically for Tier-4 languages. Can they get one with the released cone code by changing only lambda_xl?
items.answer: No. The cross-lingual term averages margins over all non-English languages equally, so raising lambda_xl increases breadth across all of them rather than for Tier 4. To target Tier 4 they would need to restrict or reweight the language set in that term.
rubric: Asserts that changing lambda_xl alone will not target Tier 4.
Explains that lambda_xl weights a uniform average over all non-English languages, so the language set in the cross-lingual term must be restricted or reweighted.

items.question: The Discussion asserts refusal geometry is effectively one-dimensional cross-lingually, with CL-RepInd as the tool for testing this. What feature of Eq. 3 makes high CL-RepInd values unsurprising, and so a weak test of the claim?
items.answer: No term in Eq. 3 rewards directions for separating different languages. Each direction is pushed toward a high average cross-lingual margin, so all of them tend to load on the same easily separated languages. Orthonormality constrains the directions in activation space, not their per-language margin profiles. High correlations are therefore what the objective tends to produce.
rubric: States that the objective contains no pressure toward distinct cross-lingual profiles, since all directions are rewarded for the same average margin.
Explains that orthonormality does not prevent correlated margin profiles, so high CL-RepInd is expected and weakly supports one-dimensionality.

items.question: Suppose Tier-4 languages had shown high silhouette and probe AUC but first principal angles near 90° to English. Would the Discussion's description of Tier-4 failure as 'upstream, not directional' fit?
items.answer: No. Harmfulness would then be well encoded but in directions orthogonal to the English ones. That is a directional mismatch, the very alternative the Discussion rules out. An upstream account requires weak separation itself.
rubric: Asserts that the 'upstream, not directional' description would not fit (it would be contradicted).
Explains that strong separation in subspaces orthogonal to English indicates a directional failure rather than weak upstream encoding.

items.question: If lambda_xl had been tuned separately for each model, which comparison involving the cone figures (Figures 5–6 and 10–11) would lose validity?
items.answer: The comparison of cone margins, quality curves and CL-RepInd across Llama, Qwen and Aya would lose validity. Differences between models could then reflect a different trade-off between English fidelity and cross-lingual breadth, not differences in model geometry. This is why the paper fixes the weighting.
rubric: Identifies cross-model comparison of the fitted cones as compromised.
Explains that lambda_xl sets the English-versus-cross-lingual trade-off, so per-model tuning confounds model differences with weighting choices.

items.question: If the Tier-4 back-translation bias were severe, which rows of Figure 9 would inherit it, and which would not?
items.answer: Row 3, the per-language behavioral labels, would inherit it, because those labels come from back-translated, WildGuard-judged Tier-4 responses. Rows 1, 2 and 4 use activations and an English-derived refusal direction. They do not depend on Tier-4 generations or their back-translation.
rubric: Identifies the behavioral label row (row 3) as inheriting the bias.
States that the activation-based rows (1, 2, 4) are unaffected because they use activations and the English r-hat, not Tier-4 back-translated text.

items.question: If the English harmfulness probe failed (AUC near chance) at a given layer, which values in Figure 4 would become uninterpretable, and why?
items.answer: Every non-English language's principal angle at that layer would become uninterpretable. Each angle is measured against the English subspace, which would then be built from probe weights that capture no harmfulness. A shared reference affects all comparisons at once.
rubric: Asserts that all languages' angles at that layer become uninterpretable.
Explains that every angle uses the English subspace as a common reference, so a meaningless English subspace invalidates them all.

items.question: Does the finding that harmfulness subspaces are not cross-lingually universal contradict the prior result of Wang et al. that English refusal directions transfer across languages? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled: the finding does not contradict the prior result. The paper measures probe-derived harmfulness subspaces, not refusal directions, and it reports that harm and refusal signals are decoupled. It also does not test whether refusal directions transfer causally.
rubric: Answers not settled (or states that there is no contradiction).
Explains that harmfulness subspaces and refusal directions are different objects (decoupled), and refusal transfer is not causally tested.

items.question: Does plotting principal angles against normalized depth show that the same normalized depth corresponds to the same processing stage in Llama, Qwen and Aya? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Normalization is a convenience that puts models with different layer counts on a shared axis. The paper gives no evidence that equal fractions of depth perform the same computation.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that normalization only aligns axes across different layer counts and is not evidence of functional correspondence.

items.question: Does the paper show whether romanizing Hindi prompts changes harmful-harmless separation in the model's representations? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. All geometric figures (silhouette, probe AUC, principal angles, Figure 9) use the standard-translation condition. Transliteration is analyzed only behaviorally.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the representation-level analyses are reported only for standard translation.

items.question: Does the paper establish that every harmless counterpart is actually harmless? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Human reviewers checked that sentence structure and length were preserved, but the paper does not report checking harmlessness. That property rests on GPT's benign substitutions.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that human verification covered structure and length only, not harmlessness.

items.question: Does the 100% WildGuard–human agreement show that the coherence filter correctly separates usable from unusable responses? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The spot-check validates WildGuard's refusal judgments on scored responses. It says nothing about whether responses the filter excluded, or kept, were correctly classified.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the spot-check targets the judge's refusal labels, not the coherence filter's decisions.

items.question: Does the decline of within-language probe AUC with tier (Figure 3) show that a probe trained on English activations would fail on Tier-4 activations? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Each probe is trained and tested within its own language, so Figure 3 measures decodability, not whether an English probe transfers. No cross-lingual probe test is reported.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the probes are within-language, so cross-lingual probe transfer is not measured.

items.question: If the coherence filter's minimum length were raised from 20 to 200 characters, could a model's Hindi standard-translation ASR change?
items.answer: Yes. More responses would be flagged incoherent and excluded, which changes the set of responses that ASR is computed over.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that the filter decides which responses enter the ASR computation, so a stricter length threshold changes that set.

items.question: If the coherence filter's minimum length were raised from 20 to 200 characters, could a model's Hindi probe AUC change?
items.answer: No. Probes are trained on prompt activations at the last post-instruction token, which involve no generated responses, so the filter never touches them.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that probe AUC uses prompt activations, not generated responses, so it is independent of response filtering.

items.question: If both the 'all' and the 'unknown' probe weight vectors for a language and layer were multiplied by 10, would that language's harmfulness subspace or its dimension k change?
items.answer: No. Uniform scaling multiplies all singular values by the same factor and leaves the singular directions unchanged, so the spectral-mass fractions, k and the subspace stay the same.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that uniform scaling leaves singular directions and relative spectral mass unchanged, so k and the subspace stay the same.

items.question: If only the 'unknown' probe's weight vector for a language and layer were multiplied by 10, could that language's harmfulness subspace or its dimension k change?
items.answer: Yes. Scaling one column changes the relative singular values and the top singular direction. The share of spectral mass can therefore cross the 95% threshold, changing k, or the retained direction can shift toward the scaled column.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that non-uniform scaling alters the relative spectral mass and singular directions, which can change k or the subspace.

items.question: If one cone direction's margin were doubled in every non-English language, would its CL-RepInd with another direction change?
items.answer: No. CL-RepInd is a Pearson correlation, which is unchanged when one vector is multiplied by a positive constant.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that Pearson correlation is invariant to uniform positive scaling of one vector.

items.question: If one cone direction's margin were doubled only in the Tier-4 languages, could its CL-RepInd with another direction change?
items.answer: Yes. Changing only some entries alters the shape of the per-language margin vector, not just its scale, so the Pearson correlation can change.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that changing a subset of languages alters the vector's pattern, which Pearson correlation is sensitive to.

items.question: Suppose harmful activations in a language became more spread out within their class, while every point stayed on the correct side of a hyperplane that perfectly separates the classes. Would the silhouette score change?
items.answer: Yes, it would fall. Silhouette depends on how compact each cluster is relative to the distance between clusters, so greater within-class spread lowers it.
rubric: Answers yes (silhouette decreases).
Explains that silhouette is sensitive to cluster compactness and spread.

items.question: Suppose harmful activations in a language became more spread out within their class, while every point stayed on the correct side of a hyperplane that perfectly separates the classes. Would probe AUC change?
items.answer: No. A linear probe can still separate the classes perfectly, so its AUC stays at its maximum. Probe accuracy needs only a separating hyperplane, not compact clusters.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that linear separability is preserved, and the probe needs only a separating hyperplane, not tight clusters.

items.question: Would changing lambda_cone alter the fitted N=1 refusal cone?
items.answer: No. The cone-spread term orders pairs of basis directions by English margin, and a single direction has nothing to be ordered against. The term is inactive, so its weight has no effect.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that the cone-spread term compares successive directions and is vacuous with only one direction.

items.question: Would changing lambda_cone alter the fitted N=5 refusal cone?
items.answer: Yes, it could. With five directions, the cone-spread term penalizes ordering violations among them, so its weight changes the optimization and can change the fitted basis.
rubric: Answers yes (it can change).
Explains that with several directions the ordering penalty is active, so its weight shapes the solution.

items.question: Suppose a model answers a Tier-4 harmful prompt by translating the prompt into English instead of carrying out or refusing the request. How does the pipeline score this response, and what does that do to the cell's ASR?
items.answer: The response is in English, longer than 20 characters and valid Unicode, so it passes the coherence filter. WildGuard does not see a refusal, so the response counts as an attack success. Such behavior inflates ASR without any harmful content being produced, because the filter checks form, not whether the response is relevant to the request.
rubric: States the response is counted as an attack success (compliant) and so raises or inflates ASR.
Explains that it passes every coherence check (English is accepted, long enough, valid Unicode) and that WildGuard only checks for refusal, not for relevance or harmful content.

items.question: Appendix E renders the same harmful request in about 26 Chinese characters versus about 79 English characters. How could the coherence filter's 20-character minimum bias Chinese ASR relative to English ASR, and why?
items.answer: A short Chinese refusal can carry the same content as an English refusal in far fewer characters, so it is more likely to fall below 20 characters and be excluded. Removing disproportionately many short refusals leaves a scored set skewed toward compliant responses, which inflates Chinese ASR relative to English. This assumes ASR is computed over the responses that remain after filtering.
rubric: States that Chinese refusals are excluded more often, biasing Chinese ASR upward relative to English.
Explains that Chinese packs the same content into fewer characters, so terse refusals fall under the fixed 20-character threshold more often.
Notes the condition that ASR is computed over the filtered (remaining) responses.

items.question: The paper says translationese introduces semantic drift. How could this drift raise translationese ASR without any weakening of the model's safety behavior?
items.answer: Repeated round-trip translation can soften or lose the harmful part of a request, as when 'harm' is dropped. The prompt may then no longer be harmful, and the model's non-refusal of a benign request still counts as an attack success. The higher ASR would then reflect changed prompt content, not a bypass of safety.
rubric: States that ASR can rise because drifted prompts may no longer be (as) harmful, so compliance is appropriate rather than a jailbreak.
Explains that the refusal-based metric counts any non-refusal on a prompt from the harmful set as a success, regardless of whether the drifted prompt is still harmful.

items.question: When would CL-RepInd between a cone direction and another direction be undefined or meaningless, even if both directions were well fitted?
items.answer: CL-RepInd is a Pearson correlation across per-language margin vectors. If one direction's margin is nearly the same in every non-English language, its margin vector has almost no variance. The correlation is then undefined, or it is driven by tiny noise fluctuations, so it says nothing about shared cross-lingual structure.
rubric: Identifies the case where a direction's per-language margins are (nearly) constant across languages.
Explains that Pearson correlation needs variance, so near-zero variance makes it undefined or dominated by noise.

items.question: Suppose Google Translate returned some words of a code-switching span unchanged, in English, for certain languages. How would that undermine reading code-switching's tier stability as robustness?
items.answer: Code-switching translates only the short differing span. If that span stays in English, the code-switched prompt is identical or nearly identical to the English prompt, so its ASR will sit near the English baseline. Apparent tier stability would then reflect failed translation, not safety that holds across languages. This is most likely where translation into the language is weakest.
rubric: States that the code-switched prompts would collapse toward the English prompt, so ASR stays near the English baseline and tier stability becomes an artifact.
Explains that only the differing span is translated, so leaving it untranslated leaves essentially no non-English content.

items.question: The paper says b0 has the largest English margin 'by construction'. Under the canonical settings (lambda_cone=5, lambda_xl=1), when could this fail, and why?
items.answer: The ordering is enforced only by a soft ReLU penalty weighted by lambda_cone. That penalty is added to the English-margin and cross-lingual-margin terms. If letting a later direction exceed b0's English margin buys enough English or cross-lingual margin to outweigh the penalty, the optimizer can accept the violation. A run limited to 400 steps also need not fully converge.
rubric: States that b0 is not strictly guaranteed to have the largest English margin; ordering can be violated.
Explains that the ordering is a finite, weighted ReLU penalty traded off against the margin terms (including the cross-lingual term), not a hard constraint.

items.question: Why is comparing two perturbations within one language and one model, such as Hindi standard translation versus Hindi translationese, more controlled than comparing two languages within one model? What caveat remains?
items.answer: Within one language and model, the refusal style, the target language of responses, and the NLLB back-translation path into English are all held fixed, so mainly the prompt varies. Across languages, back-translation quality and filter behavior differ. A caveat remains: some perturbations can change the language or script the model replies in, such as English replies to code-switched prompts or romanized replies to transliterated ones. That changes the judging path.
rubric: States that the within-language comparison holds the judging pipeline (back-translation language and quality, refusal style) fixed so only the prompt changes.
Notes the caveat that perturbations can shift the response language or script, altering the coherence or back-translation path.

items.question: Why can a nonzero ΔASR for Spanish, a Tier-1 language, not be attributed entirely to the model behaving differently in Spanish?
items.answer: The English baseline responses are scored by WildGuard directly. Spanish responses are first back-translated by NLLB-200 and checked against Spanish language detection. The ΔASR therefore mixes any change in the model's behavior with a change in the measurement pipeline.
rubric: States that the ΔASR partly reflects measurement differences, not only model behavior.
Explains that non-English responses pass through back-translation (and language-specific coherence checks) while the English baseline does not.

items.question: The paper argues transliteration reflects a realistic input distribution. Why does that argument apply to the romanized Chinese condition but not to the Latin-Cyrillic French condition?
items.answer: The realism argument rests on romanized text being common in informal online writing, which covers non-Latin languages rendered in Latin script, such as Chinese. French written phonetically in Cyrillic letters is described only as the 'analogous operation in the opposite direction', not as an established user practice. The French condition is therefore a purely adversarial stress test.
rubric: States that the realism argument fits romanized Chinese but not Latin-Cyrillic French.
Explains that realism rests on romanization being common informally, whereas Latin-Cyrillic rendering of Romance languages is only justified as an analogous adversarial operation.

items.question: Why can the code-switching condition not be built, as specified, for a harmful prompt that has no harmless counterpart?
items.answer: Code-switching translates the contiguous span in which the harmful prompt differs from its harmless partner. Without a partner, no differing span is defined, so there is nothing that identifies which words to translate.
rubric: States that code-switching cannot be constructed as specified without the harmless counterpart.
Explains that the translated span is defined as the contiguous difference between the harmful and harmless prompts.

items.question: The paper notes that translation quality into Tier-4 languages is lower. Why should Tier-4 code-switching prompts be less exposed to this problem than Tier-4 standard-translation prompts, and what risk remains?
items.answer: In code-switching only the short differing span is machine-translated, so translation errors can affect only a few words, while the shared context stays in correct English. Standard translation exposes the entire prompt to errors. The remaining risk is that those few words carry the harmful content, so a mistranslation there can still change what is being asked.
rubric: States that code-switching prompts are less affected because only the short differing span is translated and the rest stays in English.
Notes the residual risk that the translated span is exactly the harmful content, so errors there can still alter the request.

items.question: Why does high within-language harmful-harmless separation (high probe AUC and silhouette) not by itself predict a low ASR in that language, by the paper's own findings?
items.answer: Probe AUC shows that harmfulness is linearly recoverable, not that the model uses it. The harmfulness subspace can lie far from English. The paper also finds harm and refusal signals geometrically decoupled. Harm can therefore be well represented without the refusal behavior firing.
rubric: States that high separation does not guarantee refusal or low ASR.
Gives the reason: decodable is not the same as used, and/or harm and refusal signals are decoupled, and/or the subspace can lie far from the English one.

items.question: If the Discussion's claim that Tier-4 failure is 'upstream, not directional' is correct, should a team prioritize strengthening steering along the English refusal direction, or improving how Tier-4 inputs separate harmful from harmless? Why?
items.answer: They should prioritize improving Tier-4 harmful-harmless separation in the representations, for example through better Tier-4 data. 'Upstream' means the harm signal is weak before refusal machinery could act. Steering along the refusal direction works downstream and does not fix a missing harm distinction. The diagnosis is correlational, so this is a hypothesis to test, not a guarantee.
rubric: Chooses improving Tier-4 harm representation or separation over strengthening English refusal-direction steering.
Explains that 'upstream' locates the failure in weak harm separation before refusal, so a downstream refusal intervention would not address it.

items.question: A team rerunning Minionese wants to cut generation cost without changing any reported ASR. Can they skip generating responses to harmless prompts? What might they still need?
items.answer: Yes for ASR: Eq. 1 sums only over harmful prompts, so harmless responses never enter any ASR cell, and the geometric measures use prompt activations, not responses. They may still need English harmless responses if the complied set used to compute the refusal direction r-hat includes them. They would also lose any check of over-refusal.
rubric: States that skipping harmless generation leaves all ASR values unchanged because ASR uses only harmful prompts.
Notes that English responses (possibly including harmless ones) may still be needed to build the refused and complied sets for r-hat.

items.question: A team wants to estimate vulnerability to homoglyph substitution, a future-work attack type, using Minionese's existing Latin-Cyrillic French and Spanish results. Is this a valid proxy? Why?
items.answer: No. Latin-Cyrillic transliteration is a phonetic rendering that keeps pronunciation but produces visibly different text, such as 'Рэдигез' for 'Rédigez'. Homoglyph substitution keeps visual appearance instead. Those results also cover only the two Romance languages.
rubric: States it is not a valid proxy.
Explains that transliteration preserves pronunciation, not appearance, yielding visibly different strings, unlike lookalike homoglyphs (optionally noting it covers only Spanish and French).

items.question: An auditor suspects a model's safety keys on harmful words written in their native script. Which Minionese comparison tests this, and over which languages?
items.answer: Compare transliteration ASR with standard-translation ASR, which keeps phonetic content while changing script. Only the non-Latin-script languages (Chinese, Arabic, Russian, Korean, Japanese, Hindi) qualify, because romanization actually removes their native orthography. For non-Romance Latin-script languages the transliteration prompt is unchanged, and the Romance languages switch into Cyrillic rather than out of their native script.
rubric: Identifies the transliteration-versus-standard-translation comparison.
Restricts it to the non-Latin-script languages, because only there does romanization remove the native script.

items.question: A team adds a fifth perturbation, phonetic perturbation, while keeping Minionese fully crossed. How many new prompts must they create, and what is the new benchmark size?
items.answer: Full crossing applies the new perturbation to all 385 pairs (770 prompts) in all 18 languages. That gives 385 × 2 × 18 = 13,860 new prompts and a total of 385 × 2 × 5 × 18 = 69,300.
rubric: Gives 13,860 new prompts and a total of 69,300.
Explains that full crossing requires applying it to every harmful and harmless prompt in every language.

items.question: A team builds a version of Minionese whose Tier-4 prompts are written by human translators. Which of the paper's stated caveats does this remove, and which remain for Tier-4 ASR?
items.answer: It removes the Google Translate confound on the prompts: variable translation quality and systematic errors in the inputs. It does not fix scoring. NLLB-200 back-translation of Tier-4 responses still degrades, WildGuard remains the single judge, tier remains an imperfect proxy, and the models are still 8B-scale.
rubric: States that the Google Translate prompt-translation confound is removed or reduced.
States that the back-translation (NLLB) bias for Tier-4 responses remains, optionally with the single-judge and tier-proxy caveats.

items.question: Besides Figure 3 itself and the principal angles, which figure would lose its basis if the within-language probes for Tier-4 languages turned out to be unreliable, and why?
items.answer: Figure 2's silhouette scores would lose their basis. They are computed in the harmfulness-subspace-projected stream, and that subspace is built from the language's probe weights. If those probes are noise, the projection is arbitrary, so low silhouette could reflect a bad subspace rather than overlapping representations.
rubric: Identifies the silhouette scores (Figure 2).
Explains that silhouette is computed in the subspace derived from the probe weights, so unreliable probes make the projection uninformative.

items.question: If the refusal direction were recomputed separately for each language from that language's refused and complied responses, which property claimed in the Section 5.2 Synthesis would be lost, and what new confound would enter?
items.answer: The claim that the views can be compared directly across languages without re-deriving reference objects would be lost, because each language would have its own reference. The per-language refused and complied labels would also come from back-translated WildGuard judgments, which would bring the Tier-4 back-translation bias into the geometry.
rubric: States that direct cross-language comparability against a shared English reference would be lost.
Notes that per-language behavioral labels would bring the back-translation and judge biases (especially for Tier 4) into the refusal reference.

items.question: Suppose Tier-4 ASR had been as low as English while Tier-4 probe AUC stayed near chance and silhouette near zero. What would that imply for explaining Tier-4 jailbreaks by weak harmful-harmless separation?
items.answer: It would undercut that explanation. The model would refuse appropriately despite no linear harm separation, so weak separation could not be what lets jailbreaks through. The 'upstream' account would lose its behavioral counterpart. The refusals could still come from nonlinear encoding, which probes cannot rule out.
rubric: States that it would weaken or undercut the weak-separation ('upstream') explanation of Tier-4 jailbreaks.
Explains that refusal would occur without linear separation, so low separation would not be sufficient to cause failure (nonlinear encoding remains possible).

items.question: Suppose Tier-1 non-English languages showed first principal angles near 90° to English while their ASR stayed near the English baseline. Would that undermine the paper's warning about interventions calibrated on English? Why?
items.answer: No. The warning concerns interventions that act only on English-identified directions, not the model's native behavior. A model can refuse well in a language whose harmfulness subspace is far from English, and an English-calibrated intervention would still miss those directions. With harm and refusal reported as decoupled, native refusal and subspace alignment are separate questions.
rubric: States the warning would not be undermined.
Explains that the warning is about interventions acting on English directions, which is a separate question from native refusal behavior or ASR.

items.question: If romanizing non-Latin-script prompts had left ASR unchanged in every model, which stated purpose of the transliteration condition would find no support, and which Section 4.2.1 finding would fall?
items.answer: There would be no evidence for refusal mechanisms that operate on script or token identity rather than meaning, which the condition was designed to stress-test. The finding that transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned would also fall, at least on the non-Latin side.
rubric: Identifies the purpose of detecting script- or token-identity-dependent safety mechanisms as unsupported.
Identifies the 'transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned' finding as losing support.

items.question: Suppose Figure 9 row 2 showed a strong Tier-4 harm signal at the instruction token t_inst, while Tier-4 separation in the harmfulness subspace at the post-instruction position t* was weak. How would that refine the Discussion's 'upstream' account of Tier-4 failure?
items.answer: Harm would be recognized at the instruction token but not carried to the position where the other measures are read. The failure would then lie in propagating the harm signal rather than in encoding harm at all. 'Upstream' would mean upstream of refusal but downstream of recognition. Because the evidence is correlational, this would still be descriptive.
rubric: States that the failure would be in carrying the harm signal from t_inst to t*, not in failing to encode harm.
Notes that 'upstream' would need qualifying (downstream of recognition, upstream of refusal) and that the evidence is correlational.

items.question: The Synthesis says all four geometric views share a common English reference. Is that accurate for probe AUC? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper states that probe AUC is within-language: each language gets its own probe, independently of any English reference. Only the principal angles and the disentanglement panels are defined against English.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites that probes are trained within each language independently of English, so only angles and refusal-direction panels use the English reference.

items.question: Does Minionese measure a model's vulnerability to low-resource-language fine-tuning attacks of the kind described by Upadhayay and Behzadan or Poppi et al.? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled; the benchmark does not test this. All Minionese perturbations are prompt-level and by design need no gradient access, weights or optimization. Fine-tuning attacks appear only in related work.
rubric: Answers not settled (or not measured or out of scope).
Explains that Minionese contains only prompt-level perturbations requiring no weight access, so fine-tuning attacks are not evaluated.

items.question: If Aya and Llama diverge on some tier profile, does the paper support attributing the divergence to their pretraining data mixtures? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The models differ in alignment procedures as well as pretraining mixtures. Their refusal styles also interact with WildGuard and back-translation. With only three models and correlational results, the cause cannot be isolated.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that alignment procedures and refusal-style or judge interactions also differ between models, so data cannot be isolated as the cause.

items.question: Does the paper support the view that the sharp Tier 2–to–Tier 3 safety-regime transition appears just as strongly under code-switching? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not supported; the paper's own findings point against it. Code-switching is the most tier-stable perturbation, the one where resource-level influence is most diluted by the shared English context. A sharp tier-driven shift should therefore be weakest there. The paper does not report the regime view broken out by perturbation.
rubric: Says the claim is not supported (contradicted or not settled both acceptable, if it notes evidence points against it).
Explains that code-switching is the most tier-stable condition, with resource effects diluted by English context.

items.question: Does the paper show that its cheap, access-free perturbations are as effective as optimized attacks such as the greedy-gradient suffix attack on AdvBench? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper applies only its four perturbations to plain AdvBench prompts. It runs no gradient-based or optimized attack for comparison and cites such attacks only as related work.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that no optimized or gradient-based attack is evaluated for comparison.

items.question: Does the paper show that its geometric measures predict which individual prompts in a language will be jailbroken? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The geometric measures are aggregated per language and layer over all pairs. Behavioral labels are attached per language only descriptively, and no per-prompt link between geometry and outcome is reported. The relationship is stated to be correlational.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the measures and behavioral labels are aggregate per language (and layer), with no per-prompt analysis, and are only correlational.

items.question: If every harmful prompt fell into the HarmBench 'unknown' category, would each language's harmfulness subspace necessarily have dimension k = 1?
items.answer: Yes. The 'unknown' probe would be trained on exactly the same harmful-versus-harmless data as the 'all' probe, so the two weight columns would coincide. The stacked matrix would then have rank one, giving k = 1.
rubric: Answers yes, k = 1.
Explains that the 'all' and 'unknown' probes would be trained on identical data, giving identical weights and a rank-one stack.

items.question: If only half of the harmful prompts fell into the HarmBench 'unknown' category, would each language's harmfulness subspace necessarily have dimension k = 1?
items.answer: No. The 'unknown' probe would then be trained on a different subset than the 'all' probe, so its weights would generally point in a different direction. The stack could have two significant singular values, giving k = 2.
rubric: Answers no (k could be 2).
Explains that the two probes are trained on different data, so their weight vectors generally differ.

items.question: If Spanish were removed from Minionese, would the benchmark still contain any Latin-Cyrillic transliteration prompts?
items.answer: Yes. French is also a Romance language, and Romance languages are the ones transliterated into a Latin-Cyrillic rendering, so French transliteration prompts would remain.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that French, a Romance language, still receives the Latin-Cyrillic rendering.

items.question: If both Spanish and French were removed from Minionese, would the benchmark still contain any Latin-Cyrillic transliteration prompts?
items.answer: No. Spanish and French are the only Romance languages among the 18, and only Romance languages get the Latin-Cyrillic rendering. All remaining languages would be romanized into Latin script.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that Spanish and French are the only Romance languages, and all others are romanized.

items.question: If activations were read at the instruction token t_inst instead of the last post-instruction token t*, could a model's Hindi probe AUC change?
items.answer: Yes. Probe AUC is computed from residual-stream activations at the chosen position, and a different token position gives different activation vectors, so the linear separability of harmful from harmless prompts can differ.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that the probe is trained on activations at the chosen token position, which would be different vectors.

items.question: If activations were read at the instruction token t_inst instead of the last post-instruction token t*, could a model's Hindi standard-translation ASR change?
items.answer: No. ASR depends only on the model's greedy generations, coherence filtering and WildGuard judgments. Which token's activations an analyst reads does not alter the generation.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that ASR comes from generated responses, which do not depend on which activation position is read for analysis.

items.question: Suppose a model's English ASR rose while every Hindi prompt and Hindi response stayed exactly the same. Would its Hindi standard-translation ΔASR change?
items.answer: Yes. ΔASR is measured relative to the English baseline, so raising English ASR changes the difference, shrinking it, even though nothing about Hindi changed.
rubric: Answers yes (it would decrease).
Explains that ΔASR subtracts the English baseline, which changed.

items.question: Suppose a model's English ASR rose while every Hindi prompt and Hindi response stayed exactly the same. Would its Hindi standard-translation ASR change?
items.answer: No. Hindi ASR is computed only from that cell's harmful prompts and their judged responses, which are unchanged. It does not reference English.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that ASR for a cell depends only on that cell's responses, not on the English baseline.
